```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: Mag P, Somogyi Z, Kertenics A, Kovacs M, Szabo P, Jerzsele A.
  Exploratory Pharmacokinetic Characterization of Enrofloxacin and
  Ciprofloxacin in Plasma and Interstitial Fluid of Dogs: Nonlinear
  Mixed-Effects Modeling and PK/PD Target Attainment Analysis. Antibiotics
  (Basel) 2026;15(8):716.
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3390/antibiotics15080716> (open access)

Mag 2026 gave nine healthy male Beagle dogs a single fixed oral dose of
225 mg enrofloxacin (1.5 Baytril Flavour 150 mg tablets, target 20 mg/kg) and
measured enrofloxacin and its active metabolite ciprofloxacin in plasma and in
subcutaneous interstitial fluid (ISF) collected by in vivo ultrafiltration.
Four separate exploratory population PK models were fitted in Phoenix NLME
(FOCE-ELS), one per analyte-matrix pair. The authors state that the four were
never linked: neither plasma-to-ISF distribution nor enrofloxacin-to-
ciprofloxacin conversion is modelled. They are therefore packaged as four
independent model files that share this vignette.

All four share one structure: a one-compartment model with first-order
absorption, an absorption lag time and first-order elimination, with the
225 mg enrofloxacin dose as the input. For the ciprofloxacin models the
enrofloxacin dose is still the input, so CL/F and V/F also absorb the unknown
fraction of enrofloxacin converted to ciprofloxacin and are descriptive only
(Section 3.3). For the ISF models the output is the ISF ultrafiltrate
concentration.

```{r models}
stems <- c(
  "Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_plasma_dog",
  "Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog",
  "Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_plasma_dog",
  "Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_isf_dog"
)
labels <- c(
  Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_plasma_dog = "Enrofloxacin plasma",
  Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog = "Enrofloxacin ISF",
  Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_plasma_dog = "Ciprofloxacin plasma",
  Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_isf_dog = "Ciprofloxacin ISF"
)
mods <- lapply(stems, function(s) rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb(s)))
names(mods) <- stems
```

# Population

The models were fitted to eight dogs (plasma) and six dogs (ISF). Nine
purpose-bred intact male Beagles weighing 9.3-14.7 kg (mean 11.7 kg) were
enrolled (Section 4.1); one dog vomited 20 minutes after dosing and was
excluded, and probe failure removed two more dogs from the ISF analysis
(Section 2.1). Because the tablet dose was fixed, the analysed dogs received
15.3-21.0 mg/kg (mean 19.0 mg/kg). Plasma was sampled at 0, 10, 20 and 40
minutes and 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 24 h. ISF was collected over intervals
ending at 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 22.5 and 24 h. Each ISF concentration was assigned
to the interval midpoint minus the probe dead-volume delay
t_UF = 70 uL / 1.35 uL/min = 0.84 h (Section 4.8), and the ISF models were
fitted on that corrected clock. Body weight was screened as a median-centred
power covariate on CL/F and V/F and not retained, so the models have no
covariates.

# Typical-value profiles

The typical-value profiles follow from Table 3 alone. The closed-form time of
the peak for a one-compartment model with a lag is
`tlag + log(ka/k) / (ka - k)`, which can be compared directly with the
observed mean Tmax of Tables 1 and 2.

```{r typical}
typ_par <- tibble::tribble(
  ~model, ~ka, ~cl, ~v, ~tlag,
  "Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_plasma_dog", 0.78, 27.06, 131.35, 0.40,
  "Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog", 0.13, 12.10, 21.70, 1.47,
  "Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_plasma_dog", 0.46, 88.62, 804.76, 0.40,
  "Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_isf_dog", 0.24, 34.41, 334.12, 1.60
)
observed <- tibble::tribble(
  ~model, ~cmax, ~tmax, ~auclast, ~half.life,
  "Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_plasma_dog", 2.94, 2.88, 21.64, 5.89,
  "Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog", 3.77, 4.49, 44.93, 4.72,
  "Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_plasma_dog", 0.37, 4.50, 4.35, 5.17,
  "Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_isf_dog", 0.77, 8.91, 10.68, 5.12
)

# Closed-form AUC from 0 to 24 h of a lagged 1-cmt oral model.
auc0_24 <- function(dose, ka, cl, v, tlag) {
  k <- cl / v
  tp <- 24 - tlag
  dose / cl * (1 - (ka * exp(-k * tp) - k * exp(-ka * tp)) / (ka - k))
}
typ_chk <- typ_par |>
  mutate(
    k = cl / v,
    tmax_typ = tlag + log(ka / k) / (ka - k),
    auc_typ = auc0_24(225, ka, cl, v, tlag)
  ) |>
  left_join(observed, by = "model") |>
  mutate(
    tmax_pct = 100 * (tmax_typ - tmax) / tmax,
    auc_ratio = auclast / auc_typ
  )
typ_chk |>
  transmute(
    Model = labels[model],
    `Typical Tmax (h)` = signif(tmax_typ, 3),
    `Observed mean Tmax (h)` = tmax,
    `Typical AUC0-24 (ug*h/mL)` = signif(auc_typ, 3),
    `Observed mean AUC0-24 (ug*h/mL)` = auclast,
    `Observed / typical AUC` = signif(auc_ratio, 3)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Typical-value Tmax and AUC0-24 from Table 3 at 225 mg versus the observed means of Tables 1 and 2.")

stopifnot(
  # Shape: the printed Ka, Tlag and k place the peak where the data put it.
  all(abs(typ_chk$tmax_pct) < 20),
  # Scale: the printed CL/F gives about half the observed exposure in every
  # model (see Errata); a mis-keyed CL/F would leave this band.
  all(typ_chk$auc_ratio > 1.5 & typ_chk$auc_ratio < 3)
)
```

The printed parameters place the peak correctly in all four models (typical
Tmax within 13 % of the observed mean), but the typical AUC0-24 is only about
38-53 % of the observed mean exposure. This is a property of the printed
Table 3 values and is discussed under Errata.

# Stochastic simulation

Each model is simulated for 200 virtual dogs given 225 mg orally, on the
0.25 h grid the authors used for their Monte Carlo simulation (Section 4.11).
The grid runs to 48 h so that every simulated dog, including those with a late
peak, has a terminal phase for the half-life; Cmax and AUC are taken over
0-24 h as in the paper.
The residual error magnitudes are not reported, so the simulated
concentrations carry interindividual variability only.

```{r simulate}
ev <- rxode2::et(amt = 225, cmt = "depot") |>
  rxode2::et(seq(0, 48, by = 0.25))

rxode2::rxSetSeed(20261122)
sim <- bind_rows(lapply(stems, function(s) {
  out <- rxode2::rxSolve(mods[[s]], ev, nSub = 200, returnType = "data.frame")
  out |>
    transmute(model = s, id = as.integer(sim.id), time, Cc)
}))
```

```{r vpc-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5}
sim |>
  filter(time <= 24) |>
  group_by(model, time) |>
  summarise(
    p05 = quantile(Cc, 0.05),
    p50 = median(Cc),
    p95 = quantile(Cc, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(model = factor(labels[model], levels = labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, p50)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p05, ymax = p95), alpha = 0.25, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue4") +
  geom_point(
    data = observed |> mutate(model = factor(labels[model], levels = labels)),
    aes(tmax, cmax),
    shape = 4, size = 3, colour = "firebrick"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~model, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time after dose (h)",
    y = "Concentration (ug/mL)",
    caption = paste(
      "Line and band: simulated median and 5th-95th percentiles (200 dogs).",
      "Cross: observed mean Cmax at mean Tmax (Tables 1 and 2)."
    )
  )
```

Compare with Figures 1 and 2 (observed means) and the VPCs of Figure 4 of
Mag 2026. The simulated medians peak at the right time but below the observed
mean peak, consistent with the exposure gap above.

# NCA (PKNCA)

```{r pknca}
conc <- sim |>
  filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  mutate(model = labels[model])
dose <- conc |>
  distinct(model, id) |>
  mutate(time = 0, amt = 225)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc, Cc ~ time | model + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose, amt ~ time | model + id)
intervals <- data.frame(
  start = 0, end = c(24, 48),
  cmax = c(TRUE, FALSE), tmax = c(TRUE, FALSE), auclast = c(TRUE, FALSE),
  half.life = c(FALSE, TRUE)
)
nca <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))

reference <- observed |> mutate(model = labels[model])
cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca,
  reference = reference,
  by = "model",
  params = c("cmax", "tmax", "auclast", "half.life"),
  units = c(cmax = "ug/mL", tmax = "h", auclast = "ug*h/mL", half.life = "h"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
cmp |>
  dplyr::rename("Model" = model) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste(
    "Simulated NCA (median of 200 dogs; Cmax, Tmax and AUC over 0-24 h,",
    "half-life over 0-48 h) versus the observed",
    "means of Mag 2026 Tables 1 and 2. Starred rows differ by more than 20 %."
  ))
```

Tmax agrees within the expected scatter. The simulated terminal half-life
is compared only loosely: the paper's values come from at least three points
within 24 h, while the simulated values use a 48 h window, and in the
flip-flop ISF and ciprofloxacin models the terminal slope is set by the
slower of Ka and CL/V. Cmax and AUC0-24 are flagged in every model: the simulated
medians are 35-47 % of the observed means. Part of this is median-versus-mean (the observed exposures are skewed,
with SDs of 35-70 % of the mean), but most of it is the scale of the printed
CL/F and V/F, examined next against the authors' own simulations.

# Probability of target attainment (Tables 5 and 6)

The authors simulated 5000 dogs per model at 225 mg, ran NCA on each profile,
and reported the percentage of dogs reaching Cmax/MIC >= 8 and
AUC0-24/MIC >= 30, 40, 100 and 125 across MICs of 0.008-1 ug/mL. The same
calculation on the packaged models is below.

```{r pta-setup}
mic <- c(0.008, 0.015, 0.03, 0.06, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1)
targets <- c("cmax8", "auc30", "auc40", "auc100", "auc125")
pta_pub <- list(
  Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_plasma_dog = cbind(
    c(100, 99.9, 99.4, 95.6, 79.6, 47.2, 16.0, 2.8),
    c(100, 100, 99.8, 98.7, 93.0, 76.3, 47.2, 18.4),
    c(100, 100, 99.6, 97.3, 87.7, 65.3, 34.1, 10.2),
    c(99.9, 99.2, 95.6, 83.2, 55.7, 25.0, 5.9, 0.8),
    c(99.7, 98.6, 93.0, 76.3, 45.3, 17.0, 3.3, 0.3)
  ),
  Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog = cbind(
    c(100, 100, 100, 100, 99.1, 86.0, 19.5, 0),
    c(100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 99.5, 64.7),
    c(100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 99.9, 95.9, 25.6),
    c(100, 100, 100, 100, 99.8, 84.6, 7.4, 0),
    c(100, 100, 100, 100, 99.4, 59.2, 1.3, 0)
  ),
  Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_plasma_dog = cbind(
    c(97.6, 89.1, 64.0, 29.5, 6.7, 0.7, 0, 0),
    c(99.9, 99.1, 94.9, 80.1, 48.3, 17.4, 3.3, 0.3),
    c(99.7, 98.1, 90.5, 69.1, 34.4, 9.3, 1.3, 0.1),
    c(96.2, 78.7, 59.3, 26.1, 5.4, 0.6, 0, 0),
    c(93.5, 78.7, 48.3, 17.4, 2.9, 0.2, 0, 0)
  ),
  Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_isf_dog = cbind(
    c(99.5, 98.2, 92.3, 73.4, 18.7, 0, 0, 0),
    c(100, 99.9, 99.4, 96.6, 85.9, 62.0, 22.3, 0),
    c(100, 99.8, 98.7, 93.8, 77.8, 47.3, 6.4, 0),
    c(99.5, 97.8, 90.5, 71.3, 33.8, 0.5, 0, 0),
    c(99.2, 96.2, 85.9, 62.0, 19.7, 0, 0, 0)
  )
)

# Per-dog Cmax and AUC0-24 from the PKNCA results.
exposure <- as.data.frame(nca$result) |>
  filter(end == 24, PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "auclast")) |>
  select(model, id, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES)

# PTA (%) grid for one model; f scales exposure, which is exact for these
# linear models (equivalent to simulating a dose of f x 225 mg).
pta_grid <- function(cmax, auc, f = 1) {
  cbind(
    sapply(mic, function(m) mean(f * cmax / m >= 8)),
    sapply(mic, function(m) mean(f * auc / m >= 30)),
    sapply(mic, function(m) mean(f * auc / m >= 40)),
    sapply(mic, function(m) mean(f * auc / m >= 100)),
    sapply(mic, function(m) mean(f * auc / m >= 125))
  ) * 100
}
pta_rmse <- function(f, cmax, auc, pub) sqrt(mean((pta_grid(cmax, auc, f) - pub)^2))
best_f <- function(cmax, auc, pub) {
  stats::optimize(pta_rmse, c(0.5, 4), cmax = cmax, auc = auc, pub = pub)$minimum
}
```

```{r pta-fit}
pta_fit <- bind_rows(lapply(stems, function(s) {
  e <- exposure |> filter(model == labels[[s]])
  f <- best_f(e$cmax, e$auclast, pta_pub[[s]])
  tibble::tibble(
    model = s,
    rmse_nominal = pta_rmse(1, e$cmax, e$auclast, pta_pub[[s]]),
    f = f,
    rmse_best = pta_rmse(f, e$cmax, e$auclast, pta_pub[[s]])
  )
}))
pta_fit |>
  transmute(
    Model = labels[model],
    `RMSE at 225 mg (PTA points)` = round(rmse_nominal, 1),
    `Exposure factor reproducing Tables 5/6` = round(f, 2),
    `RMSE at that factor` = round(rmse_best, 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste(
    "Agreement of the packaged models' PTA with Mag 2026 Tables 5 and 6",
    "(root-mean-square difference over the 40 MIC x target cells)."
  ))

stopifnot(
  # The printed parameters under-predict the published PTA; the exposure
  # factor that reproduces it is about 2 in every model.
  all(pta_fit$f > 1.5 & pta_fit$f < 2.5),
  all(pta_fit$rmse_best < pta_fit$rmse_nominal)
)
```

At the stated 225 mg dose the packaged models under-predict the published PTA,
by 15-22 percentage points root-mean-square. Scaling every dog's exposure by a
single factor of about 1.8-2.2 (equivalently, simulating roughly 400-500 mg)
brings them much closer to Tables 5 and 6; the remaining misfit of
enrofloxacin ISF is the IIV question of the next section. The factor is close to the observed / typical
AUC ratio above, so the paper's own Monte Carlo simulation, its observed NCA
and its observed profiles all agree with each other and disagree with the
printed CL/F and V/F by the same factor. The printed values are kept as
published.

```{r pta-table}
pta_show <- function(s, f) {
  e <- exposure |> filter(model == labels[[s]])
  sim_grid <- pta_grid(e$cmax, e$auclast, f)
  pub <- pta_pub[[s]]
  out <- data.frame(MIC = mic)
  for (j in seq_along(targets)) {
    out[[targets[j]]] <- sprintf("%.0f (%.0f)", sim_grid[, j], pub[, j])
  }
  out |>
    dplyr::rename(
      "MIC (ug/mL)" = MIC,
      "Cmax/MIC >= 8" = cmax8,
      "AUC/MIC >= 30" = auc30,
      "AUC/MIC >= 40" = auc40,
      "AUC/MIC >= 100" = auc100,
      "AUC/MIC >= 125" = auc125
    )
}
pta_show("Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_plasma_dog", 1) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Enrofloxacin plasma, 225 mg: simulated PTA % (published Table 5 in brackets).")
pta_show("Mag_2026_ciprofloxacin_isf_dog", 1) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Ciprofloxacin ISF, 225 mg: simulated PTA % (published Table 6 in brackets).")
```

## Table 4 random-effect labels

The same PTA comparison also tests which parameter carries which IIV. For
enrofloxacin in ISF, Table 4 assigns 27.9 %CV to V/F and 119.2 %CV to CL/F.
A 119 %CV on CL/F spreads AUC0-24 over a log-SD of about 0.9, while the AUC
columns of Table 5 for ISF fall from 100 % to 0 % within a factor of about 2
in MIC, which implies a log-SD near 0.3. Reading the Table 4 values in the
reverse order of their row labels (V/F 119.2 %CV, CL/F 27.9 %CV) reproduces
Table 5 almost exactly. The packaged models keep the labels as printed; the
check below shows how to apply the alternative with `ini()`.

```{r iiv-swap}
mod_isf <- mods[["Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog"]]
mod_isf_swap <- mod_isf |>
  rxode2::ini(etalvc ~ log(1 + 1.192^2), etalcl ~ log(1 + 0.279^2))

rxode2::rxSetSeed(20261123)
swap_sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_isf_swap, ev, nSub = 200, returnType = "data.frame")
auc_trap <- function(t, c) sum(diff(t) * (head(c, -1) + tail(c, -1)) / 2)
swap_exp <- swap_sim |>
  filter(time <= 24) |>
  group_by(sim.id) |>
  summarise(cmax = max(Cc), auc = auc_trap(time, Cc), .groups = "drop")
e_isf <- exposure |> filter(model == "Enrofloxacin ISF")

swap_chk <- tibble::tibble(
  IIV = c("Table 4 as printed (V/F 27.9 %, CL/F 119.2 %)", "Reversed (V/F 119.2 %, CL/F 27.9 %)"),
  `SD of log AUC0-24` = c(sd(log(e_isf$auclast)), sd(log(swap_exp$auc))),
  f = c(
    best_f(e_isf$cmax, e_isf$auclast, pta_pub$Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog),
    best_f(swap_exp$cmax, swap_exp$auc, pta_pub$Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog)
  )
)
swap_chk$rmse <- c(
  pta_rmse(swap_chk$f[1], e_isf$cmax, e_isf$auclast, pta_pub$Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog),
  pta_rmse(swap_chk$f[2], swap_exp$cmax, swap_exp$auc, pta_pub$Mag_2026_enrofloxacin_isf_dog)
)
swap_chk |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  dplyr::rename("Exposure factor" = f, "PTA RMSE at that factor" = rmse) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Enrofloxacin ISF: Table 5 agreement under the two IIV assignments.")

stopifnot(swap_chk$rmse[2] < swap_chk$rmse[1])
```

The same reversal improves enrofloxacin plasma (V/F 111.2 %, CL/F 113.2 %,
Tlag 38.8 %) and, modestly, ciprofloxacin ISF (CL/F 103.9 %, Ka 72.1 %);
ciprofloxacin plasma, whose two values are similar, does not discriminate.
Users who want the simulation-consistent assignment can apply it with the
same `ini()` call shown above.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Exposure scale (Errata).** Table 3 CL/F and V/F at the stated 225 mg dose
  give about 2-2.6x lower exposure than the observed NCA (Tables 1 and 2) and
  about 1.8-2.2x lower than the
  authors' own 225 mg PTA simulations (Tables 5 and 6), and sit below the
  observed mean profiles of Figures 1 and 2, in all four models. Tmax is reproduced, so the
  disagreement is one of scale only. No unit reading of the paper produces a
  factor of 2, and no erratum was found (EuropePMC search, 2026-11-16). The
  packaged models carry the printed values unchanged; the factor that
  reproduces the published PTA (about 1.8-2.2) is computed above. Treat
  absolute exposures from these models with caution; the maintainers are
  asking the authors about the dose scale used in fitting.
* **Table 4 labels (Errata).** The PTA tables are reproduced much better if
  the Table 4 %CV values are read in reverse order of their row labels
  (shown above for enrofloxacin ISF). The packaged models keep the printed
  labels; the `ini()` override is shown above.
* **Residual error.** Section 4.9 names the residual error forms (combined
  additive and proportional, or additive for ciprofloxacin plasma) but no
  magnitudes are reported in the paper or its supplement (which holds only
  the bioanalytical validation). They are fixed to 0, so simulations show
  interindividual variability only. The 5th percentile bands of Figure 4 reach
  near zero, which implies a sizeable additive error that cannot be
  back-solved.
* **ISF clock.** The ISF models were fitted on a clock shifted by the probe
  delay of 0.84 h (Section 4.8), so their lag times include it. The models'
  time axis is that corrected clock, which is the physiological time of the
  ISF concentration.
* **ISF and metabolite models as depot-central models.** The ISF models
  absorb the oral dose straight into a compartment whose concentration is
  the ISF concentration, and the ciprofloxacin models absorb the enrofloxacin
  dose straight into a ciprofloxacin compartment, exactly as fitted. Their
  CL/F and V/F are descriptive and are not plasma, tissue or metabolite
  disposition parameters.
* **Body weight.** Screened and not retained (Section 2.3); recorded in each
  model's `covariatesDataExcluded`.
* **NCA reference values.** Tables 1 and 2 report means; the comparison table
  pools the simulated dogs by median, so skewed exposures make the simulated
  values somewhat lower even without the scale issue.
